newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein to replace Jordan's PM Kabariti.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein to replace Jordan's PM Kabariti.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan will replace Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti on Wednesday with the former premier who signed Jordan's peace treaty with Israel, government sources said.

They said Abdul-Salam al-Majali, 71, who as prime minister from 1993 to 1995 also oversaw Jordan's first multi-party elections for decades, was expected to announce a new cabinet and lead the government into elections scheduled for November.
Ministers were to gather for a final cabinet meeting on Wednesday morning before formally submitting the government's resignation to the king.
A cabinet reshuffle had been widely expected before the elections but the king's decision to replace Kabariti surprised some observers.
Ten days ago the monarch called on Kabariti, appointed in February last year with a mandate for sweeping economic and administrative reform, to step up the pace of change.

"I said to him if he still had the same enthusiasm, honesty, bravery, integrity and righteousness which we know he has...we will look at future issues with a new style," the king was quoted as saying.
"But if he is scared of confronting storms...we will have to think of another solution," the king added.

The king's comments, interpreted by the government as an endorsement of Kabariti, were seen by his opponents as a sign the monarch was setting a new agenda and might be seeking a new prime minister to carry it out.

Jordanian newspapers remarked this week at Kabariti's absence from the king's side during a visit to the site where a Jordanian soldier shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls and on the king's trip on Sunday to Jerusalem to pay condolences to families of the victims.
Some observers said Kabariti was unhappy at the king's decision to meet Netanyahu in Jerusalem, just one week after he rebuked him for pushing the Middle East "towards the abyss of bloodshed."

Two cabinet ministers announced their resignation from Kabariti's government in the last four months, citing Kabariti's "overbearing" style of leadership and his restricting of decision-making to an inner circle of ministers. One subsequently withdrew his resignation.
"Majali is more of a delegator, their styles are completely different," said one analyst, adding he expected Majali to head a caretaker government to see Jordan through the elections.
The king's replacement of Kabariti, 47, with Majali marks a return to an earlier generation of premiers.
"Majali's an old politician who has been around for many years," commented one former minister. "He signed the peace treaty with Israel and supervised the previous elections."
"His appointment is an indication of focussing on the peace again," he added.
He said Jordan also had good relations with Iraq during Majali's period in office. King Hussein subsequently turned against President Saddam Hussein and Kabariti was seen as spearheading that move.

Since Iraq signed a deal with the United Nations allowing it to export oil worth $2 billion every six months to buy food and medicines, Jordan's business community has been campaigning for better ties with Baghdad to help them secure contracts.
